reference.source: Standard breast surgery textbook and benign breast disease guidance
clinicalPearls: A galactocele is a milk-filled retention cyst and is the commonest benign breast lump associated with lactation
It typically presents during or shortly after breastfeeding, or on weaning, as a smooth, mobile, often non-tender swelling
The lump may fluctuate in size and can be firm if the retained milk becomes thick or inspissated over time
Ultrasound is the imaging of choice in this age group and may show a cystic lesion, sometimes with a characteristic fat-fluid level
Aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic, typically yielding milky fluid, which confirms the diagnosis and relieves the swelling
It is distinguished from a lactational abscess by the absence of the marked pain, erythema, and systemic upset of infection
Most galactoceles are managed conservatively or by simple aspiration, and breastfeeding can usually continue
A residual mass after aspiration, or bloodstained aspirate, warrants further assessment to exclude other pathology
reference.pathophysiology: A galactocele forms when a lactiferous duct becomes obstructed and milk is retained within a distended, cyst-like space. Obstruction commonly occurs when milk flow changes, such as at weaning or when feeding becomes irregular, allowing stasis and accumulation. Over time the water content of the trapped milk may be reabsorbed, leaving thicker, fatty, or inspissated contents that alter the consistency of the lump and its appearance on imaging. Because the fluid is sterile milk rather than pus, the lesion lacks the inflammatory features of an abscess unless secondary infection supervenes.
additionalDifferentials: Breast carcinoma (uncommon in this setting but must be considered for atypical features)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination in the context of recent or current lactation
Ultrasound as first-line imaging, potentially showing a fat-fluid level
Diagnostic and therapeutic aspiration, typically yielding milk
Cytology or further imaging if the aspirate is atypical or a mass persists
Core biopsy of any residual solid lesion
redFlags: Marked pain, erythema, and systemic upset suggesting a lactational abscess
A solid residual mass after aspiration
Atypical imaging features or a lump that does not resolve
reference.prognosis: A galactocele is entirely benign with an excellent prognosis; it usually resolves after aspiration or with conservative management as lactation settles, and breastfeeding can typically continue without harm.
pitfalls: Mistaking a galactocele for an abscess and undertaking unnecessary antibiotics or incision
Failing to reassess a mass that persists after aspiration
Overlooking the rare possibility of malignancy when features are atypical
Assuming any lactational lump is benign without appropriate imaging when uncertain
